# Glossary {#sec-glosario}

Terms in the book, by chapter.

## The architecture of a research article

### IMRaD {#gl-imrad}
Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion: the standard structure of research articles. → [Chapter 1](01-structure.qmd)

### Rhetorical move {#gl-move}
A unit of text with a specific communicative purpose, such as showing a gap. → [Chapter 1](01-structure.qmd)

### CARS model {#gl-cars}
Swales's Create a Research Space model of introductions: territory, niche, occupation. → [Chapter 1](01-structure.qmd)

### Research gap {#gl-gap}
What is not yet known or resolved, which the study addresses. → [Chapter 1](01-structure.qmd)

### Structured abstract {#gl-abstract}
An abstract with labelled parts: background, methods, results and conclusions. → [Chapter 1](01-structure.qmd)

### Context-content-conclusion {#gl-ccc}
Scheme for papers, sections and paragraphs recommended by Mensh and Kording (2017). → [Chapter 1](01-structure.qmd)

## Clear sentences

### Readability {#gl-readability}
How easy a text is to read, often estimated with formulas such as Flesch Reading Ease. → [Chapter 2](02-clarity.qmd)

### Topic position {#gl-topic}
The beginning of a sentence, which should hold old, linking information. → [Chapter 2](02-clarity.qmd)

### Stress position {#gl-stress}
The end of a sentence, which should hold new, important information. → [Chapter 2](02-clarity.qmd)

### Nominalisation {#gl-nominal}
A verb or adjective turned into a noun (analyse → analysis), often making sentences heavier. → [Chapter 2](02-clarity.qmd)

### Passive voice {#gl-passive}
Construction in which the subject receives the action (samples were stored). → [Chapter 2](02-clarity.qmd)

### Plain language {#gl-plain}
Clear, direct writing that the intended reader can understand on first reading. → [Chapter 2](02-clarity.qmd)

## Hedging and stance

### Hedge {#gl-hedge}
Word or phrase that softens a claim (may, suggest, possibly). → [Chapter 3](03-stance.qmd)

### Booster {#gl-booster}
Word or phrase that strengthens a claim (clearly, demonstrate). → [Chapter 3](03-stance.qmd)

### Stance {#gl-stance}
The writer's attitude towards claims and sources. → [Chapter 3](03-stance.qmd)

### Overclaiming {#gl-overclaim}
Stating more than the evidence supports, for example causal claims from correlations. → [Chapter 3](03-stance.qmd)

### Reporting verb {#gl-reporting}
Verb used to report sources (show, suggest, claim), which conveys stance. → [Chapter 3](03-stance.qmd)

## Common errors

### False friend {#gl-falsefriend}
Word that looks similar in two languages but has a different meaning. → [Chapter 4](04-errors.qmd)

### Uncountable noun {#gl-uncountable}
Noun with no plural form (research, evidence, information). → [Chapter 4](04-errors.qmd)

### Academic Word List {#gl-awl}
Coxhead's list of 570 word families frequent across academic disciplines. → [Chapter 4](04-errors.qmd)

### Collocation {#gl-collocation}
Words that habitually go together (conduct a study, draw a conclusion). → [Chapter 4](04-errors.qmd)

### Calque {#gl-calque}
Literal translation of an expression from another language (make a research). → [Chapter 4](04-errors.qmd)

## Peer review and correspondence

### Cover letter {#gl-cover}
Short letter to the editor that accompanies a submission. → [Chapter 5](05-review.qmd)

### Response to reviewers {#gl-response}
Document that answers each reviewer comment and explains the changes. → [Chapter 5](05-review.qmd)

### Major and minor revision {#gl-revision}
Editorial decisions asking for substantial or small changes before acceptance. → [Chapter 5](05-review.qmd)

### Politeness strategies {#gl-politeness}
Linguistic choices that soften requests and criticism. → [Chapter 5](05-review.qmd)

### Rebuttal {#gl-rebuttal}
Reasoned disagreement with a reviewer's comment, supported by evidence. → [Chapter 5](05-review.qmd)

## Presenting and networking

### Signposting {#gl-signposting}
Phrases that tell the audience where they are in a talk. → [Chapter 6](06-presenting.qmd)

### Word stress {#gl-wordstress}
The syllable pronounced with more force in a word (aNALysis). → [Chapter 6](06-presenting.qmd)

### Elevator pitch {#gl-pitch}
A 30-second summary of who you are and what you research. → [Chapter 6](06-presenting.qmd)

### Clarification request {#gl-clarification}
A phrase used to check you have understood a question. → [Chapter 6](06-presenting.qmd)

### Linguistic inequality {#gl-inequality}
The extra costs that the dominance of English imposes on non-native speakers in science. → [Chapter 6](06-presenting.qmd)
